children: The dialogue here is a kind of pantomime between husband and wife. Bloom knows of Molly’s affair with Boylan. Molly took the letter from Bloom and hid it under her pillow. Bloom sees the letter is open now and asks who it is from, knowing full well it was from Boylan. But before she can say Bloom thinks, “Bold hand. Marion.” “Bold hand” is how Bloom knows the letter is from Boylan. Joyce lets us into Bloom’s thoughts. On the surface Bloom and Molly have a simple conversation but it takes on epic proportions given the rest of the novel. Molly will give her soliloquy at the end of the novel from the bed she’s in here and will think of Bloom at the end as she falls to sleep making him the comic hero after all.

8681499.fragment: Yes, she said. There’s nothing smutty in it. Is she in love with the first fellow all the time?

range.content: Yes, she said. There's nothing smutty in it. Is she in love with the first fellow all the time?

8681499.twitter_share_message: “The use of conversational implicature in “Calypso” builds suspense between Poldy and Molly. The …” —@Genius

children: The use of
conversational implicature

in “Calypso” builds suspense between Poldy and Molly. The incongruous ‘There’s nothing smutty in it’ implies they’ve had a previous conversation or there’s a tension between them about smut! We don’t know what it refers to but know it refers to something, one of many hiatuses in “Calypso”.
PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Isn’t the question of smuttiness just part of Poldy and Molly’s relationship as sexually open and comfortable with each other (to some degree; infidelity is no
huge

secret between them both, and Poldy is pretty chilled and accepting about Molly’s sexual transgressions, esp. in “Ithaca”)? I don’t think Poldy cares at all whether his wife reads “smut”; I always thought that the reason she tells him there’s no smut is to warn him against wasting his own time reading it. We know that Poldy likes smut, and it seems Molly does too. So when she says, ‘There’s nothing smutty in it’, she’s actually expressing her frank disappointment. At a time when smut was relatively difficult to come by, people would direct people to the good stuff and warn them away from the bad stuff. It’s also possibly a comment on the charges of obscenity levelled against
Ulysses
, and its being the eventual focus of an obscenity trial: the hypocrisy of readers seeking smut out and then being “shocked” when they find it.

I think you make a good point about them having had a conversation about the same book before, presumably at another period in her reading it, and about all the unseen implied exchanges that exist between these characters. I’m not convinced that this specific exchange is a very good example of conversational implicature—if at all, strictly speaking. There’s something different, I feel, between the linguistic elements and functions of implicature (processing bits of language in practical ways that don’t necessarily follow logically from their grammatical construction) on the one hand, and on the other the fact that people will refer implicitly to past conversations and habits. Still, it is useful to illuminate the ways that
Ulysses

manages to mimic realistic interactions, where people don’t deal in exposition about why they are saying what they are; and conversational implicature is indeed one of those things we use effortlessly all the time without realising it.
Anyway. There is a nice awareness here of how dialogue and characterisation works in
Ulysses
, and this chapter in particular.
